author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Configure a dance mat, wheel, or arcade stick for one PS2 title
summary: Identify the title's expected peripheral, test Android events, build one scoped dance-mat, wheel, or arcade profile, and verify simultaneous input and safe feedback behavior.
heroAlt: PCSX2 Pop'n Music input configuration illustrating a title-specific mapping for a nonstandard PS2 rhythm peripheral

sourceLabels.pcsx2-controllers-current: PCSX2 mappings, profiles, ports, and peripherals

blocks.text: Start from the title's expected peripheral

Identify the device from Android's raw event view before choosing an emulated peripheral. Record buttons, hat directions, analog axes, resting values, pedal ranges, and whether a wheel reports separate or combined pedals. Then consult the game's manual for its expected PS2 device and port. Build a profile for that title only; a dance mat, wheel, and arcade stick require different validation even when Android labels each as a gamepad.

Do not enable force feedback or guess an emulated peripheral merely because basic buttons respond. An incorrect wheel mode can swap pedals, center steering at the wrong value, or request effects an adapter cannot safely represent. Likewise, converting a dance mat to analog directions can suppress opposing steps that rhythm games intentionally read together.
Document device type and game requirements

items: Exact game region and supported peripheral identified.
Physical device produces stable Android events.
Shared ordinary-controller profile exported before special mapping.
Record the peripheral's raw buttons, hat, axes, resting values, and USB descriptor before selecting any emulated PS2 device type.
Use the game's calibration or practice mode to test the hardest simultaneous mat step, wheel-and-pedal range, or stick diagonal.
1. List every control required by the game's calibration or test screen.
2. Choose the matching emulated PS2 peripheral type when the app supports it.
3. Map dance directions, wheel axes and pedals, or arcade directions by observed events.
4. Test simultaneous directions and buttons required by the actual game.
5. Calibrate neutral, endpoints, and dead zones for analog hardware only.
6. Enable feedback only when device, emulated type, and title explicitly support it.
7. Assign the finished profile to this exact game entry.
8. Open an ordinary title and prove the shared controller map remains untouched.

blocks.text: For a mat, press adjacent and opposite panels together and verify independent digital states. For a wheel, plot center, both locks, each pedal, and release values before setting saturation. For an arcade stick, test cardinals, diagonals, and rapid neutral returns. These traces reveal hardware capability; the game profile should translate them without inventing missing inputs.

Run the title's own calibration or practice mode, then test its hardest simultaneous input. Reconnect the peripheral, cold-launch the game, and confirm the same port and profile are selected. Launch a normal DualShock title afterward to prove the special device did not replace the shared pad mapping or occupy another player's slot.

items: The game's own calibration or test screen recognizes every required input.
Simultaneous actions do not cancel because of keyboard-style limitations.
Unsupported feedback or pressure features are left disabled and documented.
Attach the raw event chart to the final profile so unsupported feedback, pressure, or combined-axis behavior is explicit rather than guessed.
Power-cycle the peripheral and cold-launch the target serial; it must recover the same port while a DualShock title keeps the standard pad.
Wheel buttons work but steering does not: verify the emulated wheel type and axis.
Dance directions cancel in pairs: the device may expose keyboard rollover limits.
Arcade diagonals skip: inspect X/Y digital mapping and neutral return.
Feedback behaves incorrectly: disable it before trying a matching documented type.

blocks.text: Return the target serial to the ordinary controller profile and remove the special-device association. Restore the recorded center, dead-zone, and feedback settings before unplugging the hardware. Keep the raw event capture and unsupported-feature notes; they distinguish an adapter limitation from an emulator regression during future testing.
Special peripherals are title and protocol specific

Special peripherals often expose vendor-specific descriptors and incomplete Android mappings. A working button set does not prove PS2 protocol equivalence, pressure support, or force feedback. Prefer a documented partial profile over fabricated controls, and retest when changing adapters, USB hubs, Android versions, or the game's regional release.
